records.name: Zimbabwe
records.summary:
Zimbabwe is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2006 Criminal Law Act criminalises sodomy (up to 1 year — a lighter formal penalty than neighbours, though indecency provisions add exposure), and Amnesty's 2024 report documents shrinking civic space threatening LGBT organising (GALZ operates under pressure; its offices have been raided historically). There is no legal gender recognition, political rhetoric is hostile, and mob violence is documented — but prosecution under the sodomy law is rarer than in Zambia, and a small organised community persists openly enough to litigate.

For a visitor: statutory exposure exists but enforcement is sporadic; social hostility is the main risk.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women (sodomy and 'acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent'). (Only the opening of the profile was retrievable at fetch time.)

Amnesty International report, 9 January 2024, index AFR 01/7533/2024: 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries'. The cached copy is only the title/index page: it fixes the report's date, scope and thesis but contains no Zimbabwe-specific passages, so it cannot carry incident-level claims — treat it as the report's existence record, not its evidence.

New Zimbabwe, 9 July 2018: the health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender/non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty ('nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups'), issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. For a trans visitor: formal policy guarantees health-service access including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Mabvurira et al., 'The politics of sexual identities in Zimbabwe: A Social Work perspective?' (Int'l Journal of Humanities and Social Science, July 2012): homosexuals live secluded lives due to prejudice; argues homosexuality is 'as African as the baobab tree and as Zimbabwean as the Great Zimbabwe Ruins', tracing same-sex relations in pre-colonial and post-colonial Zimbabwe; social workers should promote social justice for the gay community.
Taylor & Francis (Journal of Homosexuality): academic article on homosexuality in Zimbabwe (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe) official site: voluntary membership organisation established 1990, now 4,000+ community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups, 4 resource centres. Services include legal support (explicitly including for 'sodomy' arrests), counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. For the record: documented local support infrastructure — legal aid and counselling reachable despite criminalisation, useful for an LGBTI traveller needing assistance.

records.name: South Sudan
records.summary:
South Sudan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The 2008 Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years), and Human Dignity Trust lists South Sudan as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. The country has barely emerged from civil war, state institutions are vestigial outside Juba, communal violence is endemic, and there is no documented LGBT community infrastructure whatsoever — no organisation can operate openly. No trans-specific case is documented because documentation itself is nearly impossible.

For a visitor: statutory risk plus a near-total absence of protective institutions.

sources.summary: US State Dept 2021 Country Report, South Sudan (SOGIE section): the law criminalizes same-sex sexual conduct — 'unnatural offenses' ('carnal intercourse against the order of nature') punishable up to 10 years if consensual and up to 14 years if nonconsensual; no reports authorities enforced the law; the law also criminalizes a male person who 'dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman'.

records.name: Somalia
records.summary:
Somalia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous countries for any LGBT person. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 3 years), but the operative reality is worse: Al-Shabaab controls significant territory and applies its interpretation of sharia, under which homosexuality and gender transgression are capital offences — executions are documented. Even in government areas, mob violence and clan-justice dynamics make any gender nonconformity lethal-risk. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, and no recourse of any kind.

For a visitor: there is no safe way to be visibly trans anywhere in Somalia.

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Somalia's criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity (up to life imprisonment under the 1964 penal code; death penalty under Sharia in some regions).

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Somalia: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 3 years); al-Shabaab enforces strict Sharia with death as possible punishment; pervasive violence and statelessness.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Somalia: criminalizes 'carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex', 3 months' to 3 years' imprisonment, no official reports of enforcement available; under local interpretations of sharia, homosexuality is punishable by death; no known state-conducted executions of that sort reported. Impunity generally remained the norm.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Somalia (archived): documents the conflict, al-Shabaab abuses, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and the death penalty under Islamic law in areas under insurgent control.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Feb 2016) on Benjamin Christman's 'Report on the Treatment of Gay Persons in Somalia' (published 2 Feb 2016): evidence that gay persons should not be returned to Somalia due to persecution risk, supporting refugee-status claims; notes Somalia's anti-homosexuality law provides up to... [report excerpt] — non-refoulement basis for LGBT asylum seekers.

Al Jazeera (Jul 2013) 'Gay Somali refugees face death threats': refugees in Kenya face threats and racist discrimination, with Al-Shabaab publicising intent to 'enforce harsh punishments' against homosexuality and senior figures claiming a 'death chamber' for gay and lesbians if returned; UN officials nevertheless pushed return — dated account of persecution driving displacement.

records.name: Antigua and Barbuda
records.summary: Antigua and Barbuda demands real caution. The High Court struck down the buggery/gross-indecency laws in July 2022, reading the constitutional bar on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity. No LGR, no anti-discrimination statute, and residual social hostility; tourist resort areas are insulated.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (Jul 2022): 'Antigua and Barbuda: High Court Decriminalizes Gay Sex' — the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court strikes down the 'sodomy' and 'gross indecency' provisions.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): in 2022 the High Court found Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 unconstitutional, decriminalising same-sex conduct, and interpreted 'sex' discrimination to include sexual orientation and gender identity. However, no explicit antidiscrimination protections exist, same-sex unions are not recognised, and trans people are particularly vulnerable because there is no mechanism to change legal gender markers - only name changes.

El País/AP (June 2023): profile of Orden David, the Antiguan LGBTQ activist who challenged the country's anti-sodomy law and won in 2022 - he had been bullied and physically attacked (struck in the head, knocked out in daylight); the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruled the law unconstitutional; six Caribbean countries still criminalise.

St Lucia Star (Dec 2019): ECADE announced court challenges to buggery and indecency laws in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia, arguing the laws stigmatise and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence.

The Advocates for Human Rights (January 2025): submission to the UN Human Rights Committee for Antigua and Barbuda listing LGBTQ+ rights issues ahead of its review — documents the open SOGI-protection questions the state still faces post-2022 decriminalisation.

records.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
records.summary: Saint Kitts and Nevis demands real caution. Part of the Eastern Caribbean decriminalisation wave (2022 court ruling); tiny population, tourist economy, no documented anti-trans violence pattern; no LGR.

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust page documents Eastern Caribbean constitutional challenges; Saint Kitts and Nevis decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2022 via such a challenge.

Nation News (Aug 2022): the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down anti-buggery laws - the ruling covering Saint Kitts and Nevis (Jamal Jeffers v Attorney General) decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): consensual same-sex conduct legal throughout the country since 2022 — the High Court in Jamal Jeffers v The Attorney General struck Offences Against the Person Act s.56 (buggery) and s.57 (indecent assault against men) as contrary to privacy and expression rights; legal gender recognition is not possible; LGBTI organisations may register.

Saint Kitts and Nevis Alliance + ECADE UPR presentation (2025): decriminalisation in 2022 after civil-society court challenge; LGBTQ+ citizens included in the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 but 'lack of tangible steps by the State'; discrimination in workplace, education, accommodation and hate speech still not illegal; LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement.

Country status page (fetched 2026-09-29): criminalisation of homosexuality rescinded in 2022; the penal code still contains no discrimination or harassment protections on sexual orientation or gender identity; same-sex unions are not recognised in any form (marriage or partnership), and same-sex households receive none of the rights afforded to opposite-sex married couples; gender identity recognition unavailable.

Tag archive (fetched 2026-09-29): Saint Kitts and Nevis collection led by 'Courts are the key to expanding LGBTQ rights in the Caribbean' and 'Lawsuits target 5 Caribbean nations' anti-gay laws' — advocacy coverage of the region's court-driven anti-sodomy-law challenges; the site tracks 66+ countries' anti-gay laws and reports no post-repeal discrimination statute for Saint Kitts and Nevis.

records.name: Dominica
records.summary: Dominica demands real caution. High Court decriminalised same-sex relations in April 2024 (fourth Eastern Caribbean state); the old law had allowed forced psychiatric commitment. No LGR; small community; no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch dispatch (24 Apr 2024): Dominica's High Court of Justice in Roseau decriminalised same-sex conduct; the piece's headline call is for all Caribbean nations to repeal similar criminal laws.

BBC (23 Apr 2024): the High Court struck sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act criminalising consensual same-sex activity as unconstitutional, on a case brought by a gay man living in Dominica; activists hailed 'a significant milestone in the ongoing struggle for LGBTQ rights in the Caribbean'.
NOTE: This is a State Department press statement page (archived, navigation only at fetch time); the underlying statement relates to Dominica.

US Mission Geneva (22 Mar 2011): statement on the Human Rights Council joint statement 'ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity', signed by 85 countries — the signatory list explicitly includes Dominica, a dated diplomatic commitment on the record.

Dominica News Online (20 Jul 2019): report of a High Court challenge to the buggery/sexual-activity laws filed by MiRiDom founder Daryl Phillip, announced at a news conference — contemporaneous evidence that the criminal provisions were under constitutional challenge five years before decriminalisation.

Erasing 76 Crimes (24 May 2013): Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire of Dominica publicly called for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and 'all forms of violence' against LGBT people, citing the Holy See's position — documented local religious-authority stance against criminalisation.
